newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-NZ's Birch says room for further tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-NZ's Birch says room for further tax cuts.

text.p: New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Friday that he saw room for further tax cuts.
"We look forward to reducing taxes very much in the future," Birch told a conference in Melbourne.
He said the economic outlook to be revealed next week "will show there is good opportunity to do it."
Birch said the ruling National government had already made a commitment to reducing income tax, which he said was still too high.
Birch said after his speech that further tax cuts could only be seen in the context of a multi-pronged objective of reducing debt, targetting social spending and cutting taxes.
"That's part of the mix and it's only part of the mix," he told Reuters.
He also confirmed that his remarks about the prospects of further cuts in income tax were separate from the government's existing committment to a second phase of tax cuts announced last December.
Birch's government implemented the first leg of a NZ$3.5 billion tax cut and social spending package in July.
An election under a new German-style proportional representation system will be held for the first time on October 12 and National is not assured of retaining power.
The pre-election Economic and Fiscal update due to be released next Thursday will give the budget outcome for 1995/96 and budget forecasts through to the year 1999/2000.
Birch said the interest rate market had factored in a two to three percentage point premium to U.S. bond yields to reflect political uncertainty leading up to the election.
But he believed the premium would begin to disappear after the election when investors realise that none of the more radical opposition economic policies were implemented.

In recent opinion polls, the ruling National party has about 35 percent support while the centre-left Labor party has about 20 percent, the economic nationalist New Zealand First party has about 20 percent and the left-leaning Alliance has about 10 to 15 percent.
It is widely expected that Labour and NZ First will be able to strike a deal after the election, but a NZ First-National coalition is seen as also possible, but less likely.
"It will be close and there's no doubt about that," Birch said.
"But not any one of those three opposition parties making those extreme statements are in a position to do anything. They would have to be in coalition and there's no unanimity between them."
Birch said in a speech in May that further tax cuts were possible over the next decade.
